lawyer: Sheikh Razzaque Ali with Munshi Ahsan Kabir, Advocates—For the Petitioner.
parties:
Lutfun Nessa ------ Petitioner
vs 
Mamataz Begum and others ------ Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
7. We have perused the application along with the annexed papers including the impugned judgment and the judgment of the trial Court. The admitted position is that both the courts below concurrently found that the plaintiff-opposite parties tendered the balance consideration within the time frame as evidenced by Exhibit 4, the Bainapatra. The further concurrent finding of the courts below is, that as the petitioner due to her difficulty could not register the necessary sale deed within 30-12-1997 extended that time till 30-5-1998 by endorsing on the reverse side of the Bainapatra Exhibit 4 and Mr Razzaque found it difficult to controvert these concurrent findings of facts. However, he urged, purely a legal point, which is that in a contract where time is the essence of the contract, the contract becomes void if the buyer does not get the sale deed registered within the stipulated time and in the instant case time expired on 30-5-1998, and thus the contract became void on and from 1-6-1998 and the plaintiff-opposite parties had no legal right to institute that suit long thereafter on 6-4-1999 for specific performance of contract because the original contract has become void. Mr Razzaque further submits that there is no Article in the First Schedule of the Limitation Act to cover such a situation. Therefore, in such a case not only balance money must be tendered within the stipulated time but the suit, if any, must also be instituted within the time frame and since the opposite parties did not do so the instant suit is barred by law. 

 9. Mr Razzaque submits that in the facts and circumstances of the case the plaintiff had no other alternative but to file the suit within 30-5-1998. In support of his contention he relied on two grounds, namely, one is that after the expiry of 30-5-1998 the contract became void and, as such, unenforceable. We have already answered that question. The other point is that the plaintiff had to institute the suit on or before 30-5-1998 because the case is not covered by any one of the Articles of the Limitation Act. To say that the suit is not governed by the law of limitation runs afoul of our Limitation Act. The statute of limitation was intended to provide a time limit for all suits conceivable. Section 3 of the Limitation Act provides that a suit, appeal or application instituted after the prescribed period of limitation must be subject to the provisions of sections 4 to 25 be dismissed although limitation has not been set up as a defence. Thus prescribed period means the period of limitation computed in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The Court's function on the presentation of a plaint is simply to examine whether, on the assumed facts, the plaintiff is within time. The Court has to find out when the right to sue accrued to the plaintiff. If a suit is not covered by any of the specific articles prescribing a period of limitation, it must fall within the residuary article. The purpose of the residuary article is to provide for cases which could not be covered by any other provision in the Limitation Act. The residuary article is applicable to every variety of suits not otherwise provided for. Article 120 of the Act is a residuary article for cases not covered by any other provisions in the Act. It prescribes a period of six years when the right to sue accrues. According to the third column in Article 120, time commences to run when the right to sue accrues. The words right to sue ordinarily mean the right to seek relief by means of legal proceedings. Generally, the right to sue accrues when the cause of action arises that is, the right to prosecute to obtain relief by legal means. Thus the suit must be instituted when the right asserted in the suit is infringed or when there is a clear and unequivocal threat to infringe that right by the defendant against whom the suit is instituted. According to Mr Razzaque, Article 113 of the Limitation Act is not attracted and there is no other Article in the Limitation Act to cover the situation. Mr Razzaque failed to assign any reason why Article 113 of the Limitation Act will not be attracted in the instant case and we also do not find any reason why Article 113 of the Limitation Act will not apply to the facts and circumstances of the case which provides for the period of limitation for specific performance of contract. In the instant case there is no dispute that time is the essence of the contract and the further concurrent finding is that balance consideration was tendered within the time frame but the defendant refused to accept the same and execute the deed. Therefore, the instant suit is nothing but a suit for specific performance of contract and there is no scope to entertain any doubt about it. The submission of Mr Razzaque is, no doubt, a noble and new one but appears to be devoid of any substance. So, in such a case limitation will run from the date of refusal of the defendant to perform his part of the promise. A suit for specific performance of a contract of sale of property is undoubtedly covered by Article 113 of the Limitation Act and limitation runs from the date of refusal to perform the obligation or his part of the contract. Be that as it may, even if the submission of Mr Razzaque is accepted that Article 113 of the First Schedule will not apply then also there is no substance in the said submission, inasmuch as in that case the residuary Article, i.e. Article 120, of the Limitation Act will apply. Therefore, in any view of the matter, the suit is not barred by limitation. Thus, we do not find any force or substance in this submission as well.
